description: The armies of the ancient Greek city-states centered on heavily armed citizen-infantry fighting in close-order formations with large round shields, spears, helmets, and body armor. These hoplites (“men-at-arms”) relied on discipline, cohesion, and mutual protection within the phalanx, where each soldier’s shield helped cover the man beside him. Although equipment, training, and battlefield doctrine varied between states such as Sparta, Athens, Thebes, and Corinth, hoplite warfare became a defining feature of Greek military culture, closely tied to civic identity, personal valor, and the defense of the polis.
